title: Tensor–adjunction form of the exchange
statement:
In the six-functor datum of
[def-fix-six-functor-datum], let $f$ be
exceptionally
admissible, and let $M\in D^b_{ctf}(X,\Lambda)$ and
$N\in D^b_{ctf}(Y,\Lambda)$. There is a canonical isomorphism

$$
Rf_*R\mathcal Hom_X\bigl(M,f^!N\bigr)
\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }
R\mathcal Hom_Y\bigl(Rf_!M,N\bigr),
$$

natural in $M$ and $N$, compatible with finite reduction, scalar
extension, and shifts.

proof.text:
First establish the actual tensor–Hom bijection, rather than take it from a definition of the operations. On any of the small ringed sites $\mathcal C$ in the datum, write $H(P,Q)=R\mathcal Hom(P,Q)$. The two cited statements give, naturally in $L,P,Q$,
$$\operatorname{Hom}(L,H(P,Q))
\cong H^0(\mathcal C,H(L,H(P,Q)))
\cong H^0(\mathcal C,H(L\otimes^L P,Q))
\cong\operatorname{Hom}(L\otimes^L P,Q).$$
The outer bijections are the global-sections identification and the middle one is internal-Hom currying. Interchanging the tensor factors gives the convention $P\otimes^L L$ used below. These bijections are the adjunction with evaluation as counit. At finite coefficients this is the ambient, uncompleted tensor–Hom adjunction; no site-perfectness assumption is made.

source.place: Tags 08JA (lemma-section-RHom-over-U), 08J9 (lemma-internal-hom); direct composition of their statements

proof.text:
At $R=\mathcal O_E$, let $P,L,Q$ be integral bounded constructible objects on a scheme $W$, and put $T=P\otimes^L_{\widehat R_W}L$, using the ordinary ambient tensor only in this paragraph. The completed tensor in the datum is
$$P\widehat\otimes^L_R L=R\varprojlim_n\operatorname{Res}_n(P_n\otimes^L_{A_n}L_n).$$
Its tower is the quotient tower of $T$: on K-flat representatives, the balancing isomorphism is $(p\otimes a)\otimes(l\otimes b)\mapsto(p\otimes l)\otimes ab$, with inverse $(p\otimes l)\otimes a\mapsto(p\otimes1)\otimes(l\otimes a)$. It commutes with differentials and quotient transitions. The constant/completed-coefficient comparison identifies this quotient limit, with its unit, with the Koszul completion of $T$ over $\widehat R_W$. It also identifies the local and Koszul completeness conditions. The integral definition makes $Q$ isomorphic to a quotient limit of its reductions; that limit is a completion by the same comparison, hence $Q$ satisfies the local completeness condition needed by the reflector. Apply the reflector's mapping property, then step 1:
$$\operatorname{Hom}(P\widehat\otimes^L_R L,Q)
\cong\operatorname{Hom}(P\otimes^L_{\widehat R_W}L,Q)
\cong\operatorname{Hom}(L,H(P,Q)).$$
Every arrow is natural and induced by the completion unit or evaluation. This proves the needed completed tensor–Hom adjunction by composing existing statements; it does not identify the two tensor objects. The Noetherian coefficient ring is $R$, the ideal is $(\varpi_E)$, and the site is small, exactly as required by the cited completion comparison and reflector.

source.place: Tag 099M (lemma-naive-completion), with algebraization.tex Tags 099B and 0A0E, and the completed-coefficient comparison of the cited node

proof.text:
Check the domain for Yoneda first at $\Lambda=A_{E,n}$. Write
$$A_{M,N}=Rf_*H(M,f^!N),\qquad B_{M,N}=H(Rf_!M,N).$$
The exceptional adjunction restricts to the finite-Tor subcategories, so $f^!N$ and $Rf_!M$ lie there. The dimension-finiteness lemma supplies nonnegative integer bounds $d_X,d_Y$ for $X,Y$ (take zero for an empty scheme). To apply finite constructible internal-Hom preservation without assuming that either scheme is separated over $k$, argue as follows for $W=X,Y$. The finite-type definition gives a finite affine cover $W=\bigcup_{i=1}^tU_i$ by spectra of finitely generated $k$-algebras; these are Noetherian by the affine Noetherian lemma. Their inclusions are separated finite-type morphisms, so the finite-Tor pullback lemma restricts both inputs with the same Tor intervals. Each $U_i$ is separated over $k$. Apply the internal-Hom corollary on $U_i$, with the single bound $d_W$, and identify its output with the restriction of $H$ by the ringed-site internal-Hom restriction statement. The resulting Tor interval $[c-b-2d_W,e-a+2d_W]$ is independent of $i$. It holds globally: restriction is exact and commutes with tensor, and a cohomology sheaf vanishing on all $U_i$ vanishes. Constructibility also assembles explicitly: intersect each finite local stratification with $U_i\setminus\bigcup_{j<i}U_j$. These form a finite disjoint locally closed constructible stratification of $W$, with the same locally constant finite restrictions; the common Tor interval bounds the nonzero cohomology degrees. Thus the definitions give bounded constructible finite-Tor internal Homs globally. Apply this argument to $(M,f^!N)$ on $X$ and $(Rf_!M,N)$ on $Y$, and apply the pro-etale direct-image theorem to the first internal Hom. Both $A_{M,N}$ and $B_{M,N}$ therefore lie in the same full category $D^b_{ctf}(Y,A_{E,n})$. For an empty cover the objects are zero. No properness or site-perfectness hypothesis is used.

source.place: Proof, construction and detection; replaces the asserted unproved detection of ambient outputs by independently established finite-Tor membership

proof.text: For $\Lambda=R=\mathcal O_E$, the exceptional adjunction again makes $f^!N$ and $Rf_!M$ integral bounded constructible. The integral internal-Hom statement, with the finite-level bounds checked by the affine-cover argument in step 3, gives $H(M,f^!N)$ and $B_{M,N}$ in $D^b_c(-,R)$, with the stated uniform finite-level Tor bounds. For $H=H(M,f^!N)$, direct image preserves derived completeness and identifies $(Rf_*H)_n$ with $Rf_*(H_n)$. If $H_n$ has Tor interval $[c,d]$, the finite pro-etale direct-image theorem bounds all these reductions in $[c,d+2d_X]$, independent of $n$, and gives constructibility. Consequently $A_{M,N}$ satisfies the integral definition, including its uniform cohomological bound. The residue-Tor theorem identifies $D^b_c(-,R)$ with $D^b_{ctf}(-,R)$, so both $A_{M,N}$ and $B_{M,N}$ are objects of the full finite-Tor category used below. This uses completed coefficient sheaves throughout, rather than a silent identification with constant-coefficient or condensed-module categories.

source.place: Proof, coefficient passage; integral completeness and uniform domain bounds supplied explicitly

proof.text:
Let $\Lambda$ now be finite or integral and $L\in D^b_{ctf}(Y,\Lambda)$. Using the adjunctions from steps 1–2, the projection isomorphism, and the two functor adjunctions, form the natural bijection $h_L$:
$$\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Hom}_Y(L,B_{M,N})
&\cong\operatorname{Hom}_Y(Rf_!M\otimes^L L,N)\\
&\cong\operatorname{Hom}_Y(Rf_!(M\otimes^L Lf^*L),N)\\
&\cong\operatorname{Hom}_X(M\otimes^L Lf^*L,f^!N)\\
&\cong\operatorname{Hom}_X(Lf^*L,H(M,f^!N))\\
&\cong\operatorname{Hom}_Y(L,A_{M,N}).
\end{aligned}$$
At the integral stage every tensor in this chain is completed tensor. For the second arrow precompose with $\operatorname{PF}_{f,M,L}^{-1}$: its direction is from $Rf_!(M\otimes^LLf^*L)$ to $Rf_!M\otimes^LL$. The projection theorem needs $M$ bounded constructible and $L$ finite-Tor, both available. All intermediate inputs to the exceptional adjunction are bounded constructible: the finite-Tor pullback lemma applies to $L$ and gives bounded constructibility of $Lf^*L$, tensor with the finite-Tor $M$ preserves it, and integral pullback and completed tensor preserve it by their integral preservation theorem. Hence the ordinary $D^b_c$ exceptional adjunction suffices here. The last arrow is the ordinary pullback–direct-image adjunction on bounded constructible objects. These checks justify every bijection without invoking the preservation summary that depends back on this item.

source.place: Proof, Step 1, all five adjunction arrows and their domains

proof.text:
Apply the fully faithful Yoneda embedding to the full category $\mathcal C=D^b_{ctf}(Y,\Lambda)$, which contains both objects by steps 3–4. The natural bijections $h_L$ identify $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal C}(-,B_{M,N})$ with $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal C}(-,A_{M,N})$. Explicitly set
$$a=h_{B_{M,N}}(1_{B_{M,N}}):B_{M,N}\to A_{M,N},\qquad
b=h_{A_{M,N}}^{-1}(1_{A_{M,N}}):A_{M,N}\to B_{M,N}.$$
Naturality in $L$ says $h_L(u)=a\circ u$ and $h_L^{-1}(v)=b\circ v$. Thus $ab=1_A$ and $ba=1_B$. The required canonical isomorphism has forward map $b$. Naturality of the five bijections in $M$ (contravariantly) and $N$ (covariantly) implies naturality of this isomorphism by the uniqueness part of Yoneda. In particular no extension-by-zero generator theorem, geometric-stalk detection, or unproved equivalence of whole sites is needed.

source.place: Tag 001P (lemma-yoneda), fully faithful embedding applied to the specified full category

proof.text: Verify the coefficient squares for this specified map by transposition. In the direction $A\to B$, the map sends a test morphism $u:L\to A$ first to its $Lf^*\dashv Rf_*$ transpose, then to its tensor–Hom transpose $M\otimes^LLf^*L\to f^!N$, then to its $Rf_!\dashv f^!$ transpose, then precomposes with $\operatorname{PF}_{f,M,L}$ and transposes tensor–Hom once more. Each transposition is a bijection. For a coefficient functor $T$, insert the comparison maps at these five places. Tensor/evaluation and unit/counit preservation, together with projection-formula compatibility, makes the composite equal whether $T$ is applied before or after these five operations. Therefore the two routes around the exchange comparison square have the same transpose and are equal. Between finite quotients use the general finite-Tor internal-Hom comparison, not the site-perfect-only clause of the elementary operation-reduction lemma; finite direct image has its finite-Tor comparison as well. For integral reduction use the arbitrary-first-variable integral Hom comparison. For exceptional inverse image use precisely the coefficient comparisons assumed in exceptional admissibility. Integral scalar extension of Hom uses its stated scalar-extension theorem. This proves compatibility of the actual exchange morphisms, rather than just their isomorphism classes.

source.place: Proof, final coefficient-comparison sentence, with the transposition composite and the finite/integral domains stated explicitly

proof.text:
The shift compatibility is checked on the same Hom bijection. Under the canonical shift identifications, for any integer $r$,
$$\operatorname{Hom}(L,A_{M,N[r]})\cong\operatorname{Hom}(L[-r],A_{M,N}),\qquad
\operatorname{Hom}(L,B_{M,N[r]})\cong\operatorname{Hom}(L[-r],B_{M,N}).$$
The five arrows for $(L,N[r])$ identify with those for $(L[-r],N)$: a tensor factor shifted by $r$ shifts the tensor by $r$, and each right adjoint's shift comparison is the transpose of the corresponding comparison for its left adjoint. The tensor–Hom comparisons have the signs of the shifted Hom complex; shifting its first variable gives $H(M[r],Q)=H(M,Q)[-r]$, while shifting its second gives $H(M,Q[r])=H(M,Q)[r]$. Both transposition routes therefore use the same signed evaluation map. In the projection definition, the proper projection map is the transpose of $(\varepsilon_p\otimes1)\circ\mu_p$, and the compact-support map is its composite with $Rp_*(\gamma)$, where $\gamma$ is the extension-by-zero tensor comparison followed by pullback composition. Shifting either tensor factor shifts each of these composites by the total-tensor convention, using $d_{C[r]}=(-1)^rd_C$; the evaluation comparison uses that same convention. The shifted composite is therefore the specified shifted projection transformation. Thus $h$ for the shifted arguments is the shifted $h$. By uniqueness in step 6 this proves the shift square for the exchange, in the second variable and, with the negative shift, in the first. Completion commutes with these identifications since its Koszul-limit construction is exact and the completion unit is natural.

source.place: Statement, shifts; direct graded transposition calculation using the specified comparisons

proof.text: Pass to the two field stages using their actual definitions. Rationalization keeps the integral objects and replaces each Hom group by its tensor product with $E$. Send the inverse pair $(a,b)$ of step 6 to its images there; their composites remain identities. The integral tensor–Hom bijection and its naturality localize, and the prescribed operations on objects and morphisms are the ones of the datum, so this gives the displayed exchange over $E$. For $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$, represent the finitely many input objects and maps over a common finite extension $E$. Define the exchange by its $E$-stage map. Step 7 identifies this representative after any larger finite extension, so its class is independent of the representative. The inverse is represented by the inverse at that same stage; naturality and the coefficient and shift equations hold over a common stage and therefore in the directed colimit of Hom groups. This supplies every coefficient stage in the statement without using a theorem on integral or field exceptional adjoints that depends back on this item.
